intro_band.agent_remit_summary: Hermes is a single-tenant personal AI agent that assists one operator with open-ended work — conversation, coding, driving a real terminal and browser, running code, scheduled cron jobs, subagent delegation, and cross-session memory and self-created skills — reachable identically through a CLI/TUI, an Electron desktop app, an editor/ACP adapter, a ~20-platform messaging gateway, and an optional HTTP surface. Its authorized tools span terminal, file ops, execute_code, web and browser automation, delegate_task, memory, skills, cronjob, and send_message, plus operator-configured MCP servers. It serves only the single operator and explicitly-allowlisted or pairing-approved messaging users, and must never serve unauthenticated callers, exfiltrate credentials, or run catastrophic commands (filesystem-root wipe, fork bomb, disk format) — an unconditional floor with no override, even under --yolo.
intro_band.agent_structure_summary: A large, mature, actively-maintained Python agent core (~2000 modules) plus an Electron/React desktop control surface that spawns and drives a loopback hermes serve backend. Terminal and execute_code pass through a layered guard in tools/approval.py — an unconditional hardline blocklist, a sudo -S guard, a 47-pattern dangerous-command detector with NFKC/ANSI normalization, per-session approval state, and optional auxiliary-LLM smart-approval — with SSRF egress checks in tools/url_safety.py, sandbox credential scrubbing in tools/env_passthrough.py, shared injection/exfil scanning in tools/threat_patterns.py, and MCP tool-description scanning in tools/mcp_tool.py. Dependencies are exact-pinned in pyproject.toml with an OSV malware pre-check on MCP packages; credentials are written atomically at 0600; the gateway authenticates messaging users via a pairing flow rather than open serving; and a 1300-file test suite includes a dedicated adversarial-security cluster. Divergences from the remit concentrate in the approval layer's behavior in non-interactive, non-gateway execution contexts.

behavior_summary: Hermes is a security-conscious agent whose controls are real and operative rather than declarative: an unconditional catastrophic-command floor, fail-closed SSRF checks, non-overridable credential scrubbing, exact dependency pinning with OSV screening, and an adversarial test suite tied to named advisories all run on the agent's path. The dominant weakness is not an absent control but a scoping gap in the one that matters most — the terminal and execute_code approval gate auto-approves dangerous (non-hardline) actions in any execution context it does not recognize as CLI, gateway, ask, or cron (a documented headless-local limitation), and the screening it does apply is pattern-based over a Turing-complete shell that execute_code's arbitrary Python sidesteps entirely. The remaining findings are calibration issues around that same axis — an opt-in aux-LLM approver, a redirect-based SSRF gap in third-party web SDKs, free-form (non-structured) action logs, and a regex-mitigated writable-memory persistence surface.

rules.rule_text: Dispatching agent work, resolving an approval, or returning agent output to a caller who is outside the configured authorization set (allowlist, pairing approval, or OS-level equivalent) MUST NOT be possible; treating a session identifier as proof of authorization is forbidden.
Any messaging platform without a configured allowlist must serve no one (fail closed).
A network-exposed adapter MUST NOT fail open (serve callers) when no allowlist / auth provider is configured.

Credentials and gateway tokens MUST NOT be passed into lower-trust child processes (shell subprocesses, execute_code, MCP subprocesses, cron scripts) except variables the operator or a loaded skill has explicitly declared as passthrough.
Secrets MUST NOT be written to logs, transcripts, error messages returned to the model, or any outbound adapter payload.
Credentials MUST NOT be committed to version control or stored in the main (shareable) config file.

rules.section: Action Boundaries — Requires Human Approval Before Execution
rules.rule_text: Any terminal command matching a dangerous/destructive pattern on a host-reaching backend MUST prompt the operator and MUST NOT execute until approved.

rules.section: Action Boundaries — Requires Human Approval Before Execution
rules.rule_text: When an approval prompt is not answered within the configured window, the action MUST be denied (fail closed).

rules.section: Action Boundaries — Requires Human Approval Before Execution
rules.rule_text: Installing or loading a third-party skill or plugin MUST give the operator a chance to review its actual code before it executes.

rules.section: Action Boundaries — Requires Human Approval Before Execution
rules.rule_text: Cron jobs that hit a dangerous-command prompt MUST default to denying it rather than silently auto-approving.

rules.section: Action Boundaries — Requires Human Approval Before Execution
rules.rule_text: Binding any local-only surface to a non-loopback interface MUST be a deliberate operator action that engages an authentication layer.

Executing a catastrophic, irreversible command (filesystem-root wipe, fork bomb, formatting a mounted device, zeroing a physical disk, piping an untrusted remote script straight to a shell) MUST be refused unconditionally — even under --yolo, approvals.mode: off, a permanent allowlist entry, or headless cron approve-mode.
Credentials or session-authorization material MUST NOT leak to any destination outside the operator's trust envelope through environment leakage, adapter logging, or transport error paths.

The desktop app MUST NOT weaken the Agent's trust rules: it MUST rely on the same backend authorization (auth gate on non-loopback binds, allowlists) and MUST NOT expose a password-only-protected remote backend to the public internet.

The desktop-launched backend MUST remain a JSON-RPC/API surface only (no unintended browser-reachable UI) and MUST stay bound to loopback unless the operator deliberately configures a remote/authenticated setup.
Sessions are isolated from one another; one session MUST NOT read another session's data or state.
Cron sessions run with a hard interrupt bound so a runaway loop cannot monopolize the scheduler.
Agent actions and decisions are recorded to durable, operator-inspectable logs.
Actions that should never be retried: a command that was denied or blocked MUST NOT be silently retried or rephrased to evade the guard.
Pairing codes and auth secrets MUST NOT be logged to stdout or persisted in world-readable files.

findings.summary: Terminal and execute_code auto-approve dangerous (non-hardline) actions in any execution context not recognized as CLI, gateway, ask, or cron.
findings.description: check_all_command_guards and check_execute_code_guard prompt only in CLI/gateway/ask contexts (or deny under cron_mode=deny); a headless local, ACP, or API-driven session falls through to approved:True. The remit requires dangerous commands on host-reaching backends to prompt and not execute until approved. Only the shell-only hardline floor still applies, so recoverable-but-destructive commands and arbitrary execute_code Python run unattended.
policy_rule_text: Any terminal command matching a dangerous/destructive pattern on a host-reaching backend MUST prompt the operator and MUST NOT execute until approved.

evidence.snippet: check_all_command_guards lines 1206-1223 — outside CLI/gateway/ask and not a cron-deny session, dangerous commands return approved:True with no prompt
check_execute_code_guard docstring (#30882) — in a purely local non-interactive non-gateway session execute_code returns approved; only the hardline floor blocks catastrophic shell commands

recommended_actions: Default the non-interactive/non-gateway path to fail-closed (deny) for detected dangerous commands and execute_code, requiring an explicit operator opt-in as cron_mode already does.
Extend the cron_mode=deny contract to all headless execution contexts (ACP, API server, batch) so no dispatch surface auto-approves.

findings.summary: Dangerous-command screening is a regex denylist over a Turing-complete shell, and execute_code's arbitrary Python bypasses the shell-pattern layer entirely.
findings.description: HARDLINE_PATTERNS and DANGEROUS_PATTERNS match normalized command strings, so shell indirection (variable assembly, decoded payloads) and Python calls (shutil.rmtree, os.remove) that never form a matching shell token evade both the dangerous detector and the catastrophic floor. The floor is the remit's unconditional-refusal control, so its pattern basis makes that refusal best-effort rather than guaranteed on host-reaching backends.
policy_rule_text: Executing a catastrophic, irreversible command (filesystem-root wipe, fork bomb, formatting a mounted device, zeroing a physical disk, piping an untrusted remote script straight to a shell) MUST be refused unconditionally — even under --yolo, approvals.mode: off, a permanent allowlist entry, or headless cron approve-mode.

evidence.snippet: HARDLINE_PATTERNS (203-225) and DANGEROUS_PATTERNS (321-427) are regexes over the command string after NFKC/ANSI normalization — indirection past the tokens is not covered
check_execute_code_guard — execute_code runs arbitrary local Python that does not pass through terminal()/DANGEROUS_PATTERNS; destructive os/shutil calls are never pattern-screened

recommended_actions: Steer host-reaching or untrusted-input deployments onto containerized backends (docker/modal/daytona) where the pattern layer is intentionally bypassed because the host is unreachable, and treat the regex guards as defense-in-depth.
Add coarse execute_code screening (AST scan for destructive filesystem/process calls) before the script's child process is spawned.

findings.summary: In approvals.mode=smart an auxiliary LLM auto-approves flagged dangerous commands, so a benign-looking framing can win approval without operator review.
findings.description: _smart_approve asks an aux model to APPROVE/DENY/ESCALATE with guidance to approve package installs, git ops, and script execution; an APPROVE verdict grants session-level approval and runs the command. It is opt-in (default manual) and escalates on uncertainty or LLM error, but a crafted or injected command dressed as routine tooling can be auto-approved on a fabricated rationale.
policy_rule_text: Any terminal command matching a dangerous/destructive pattern on a host-reaching backend MUST prompt the operator and MUST NOT execute until approved.

evidence.snippet: _smart_approve (878-922) prompts an aux LLM and maps APPROVE→auto-approve with a permissive false-positive rationale
approvals.mode=smart path (1270-1281) grants approve_session for every warning key and returns approved:True on the LLM verdict

recommended_actions: Keep smart mode off by default, document it as an isolated/disposable-environment posture, and raise every smart auto-approval as an operator alert (per the remit escalation rule) rather than a debug log line.
Require the aux verdict plus deterministic-denylist agreement before auto-approving, so an LLM APPROVE alone cannot clear a genuinely dangerous pattern.

findings.summary: web_search and web_extract rely on third-party SDKs whose redirect handling runs server-side, so the pre-flight SSRF check does not cover redirect-based bypass for those tools.
findings.description: is_safe_url validates the initial target and fails closed, and direct fetches, vision, and platform adapters re-validate each redirect, but the hosted web SDKs (Firecrawl/Tavily) follow redirects on their own servers where Hermes cannot re-check, leaving a redirect-to-internal SSRF path for those two tools. The always-blocked cloud-metadata floor still applies wherever Hermes itself resolves the host.

evidence.snippet: module docstring (15-23) — "Web tools use third-party SDKs (Firecrawl/Tavily) where redirect handling is on their servers"; redirect re-validation only covered for non-SDK fetch paths

recommended_actions: Route web_search/web_extract through an egress proxy or a Hermes-controlled fetch path that re-validates each redirect target, or restrict those tools to providers exposing redirect-chain validation.
Document the residual redirect-SSRF risk for the hosted web SDKs in the deployment guide.

findings.summary: Agent action logs are durable and redacted but free-form text rather than a structured schema, limiting automated anomaly detection.
findings.description: hermes_logging writes rotating agent.log/errors.log/gateway.log through a redacting formatter, satisfying durable operator-inspectable logging, but the free-form text format cannot drive automated detection rules and the tool-loop hard-stop is off by default (warn only). This narrows, without breaking, continuous monitoring.

evidence.snippet: three rotating text logs (agent.log/errors.log/gateway.log) with RedactingFormatter — human-readable, not a structured JSON event schema
ToolCallGuardrailConfig hard_stop_enabled defaults False — loop detection warns but does not halt unless opted in

recommended_actions: Emit a structured JSON-lines action/decision event stream alongside the human logs (tool name, args hash, approval outcome, session key) so downstream detection can parse it.
Consider enabling the tool-loop hard stop by default for headless and gateway sessions.

findings.summary: Persistent memory and agent-created skills are writable without approval and defended only by a regex threat-scan, leaving a bypassable injection-persistence surface.
findings.description: Memory and skills load into every session as secondary prompts and are written without operator approval (remit-authorized); memory_tool scans content on write and on load with the shared pattern library, but the scan is regex-based and evadable, so injected content from web/message/file ingress could persist across sessions. No vector store is involved (session search is keyword-based), so this is file-backed context poisoning, not an embedding weakness.

evidence.snippet: memory content scanned on write (strict scope, :79-80) and on load into the system prompt (:185-199, blocked entries replaced with a placeholder)
threat library is regex-based (_PATTERNS 49-115) — anchored on known vocabulary, evadable by novel phrasings

recommended_actions: Tag memory entries with the provenance of their source ingress (web / inbound message / file vs agent-authored) and quarantine externally-derived entries so they are distinguishable and reviewable.
Surface a periodic operator review of memory and skill diffs; treat the regex scan as one layer, not the trust boundary.

findings.summary: The webhook receiver and WeCom callback server default to a 0.0.0.0 all-interfaces bind rather than loopback, though both require HMAC-SHA256 signature validation.
findings.description: webhook.py and the WeCom callback config default host to 0.0.0.0, widening network exposure beyond the remit's loopback-default expectation; the engaged HMAC per-route signature check keeps the surface authenticated, so this is a hardening-default gap rather than a fail-open. The remit expects a non-loopback bind to be a deliberate operator action.
policy_rule_text: Binding any local-only surface to a non-loopback interface MUST be a deliberate operator action that engages an authentication layer.

evidence.snippet: host = wh.get("host", "0.0.0.0") — webhook receiver defaults to all-interfaces (HMAC-SHA256 signature validated at :268-277)
WECOM_CALLBACK_HOST default "0.0.0.0" — callback server binds all interfaces by default

recommended_actions: Default these receivers to 127.0.0.1 and require an explicit operator opt-in (flag/config) to bind non-loopback, consistent with the API server's insecure-bind gate.
Document that a public bind must sit behind a reverse proxy or firewall.

findings.summary: send_message can address arbitrary recipients (new E.164 numbers or DM user IDs) on enabled platforms, an outbound scope the remit leaves as an unresolved operator decision.
findings.description: The tool resolves target references including raw phone numbers and direct-message user IDs rather than restricting delivery to the originating allowlisted conversation. The remit routes outbound-recipient scope to an Open Question, so this is a capability to constrain rather than a rule violation; combined with injectable content it is a potential exfiltration or tool-misuse vector.

evidence.snippet: _parse_target_ref (354-406) accepts direct recipient references incl. E.164 phone numbers, not just the originating conversation

recommended_actions: Add a config option to constrain send_message to existing allowlisted conversations (or an explicit recipient allowlist), defaulting to reply-only.
Resolve remit Open Question #4 for this deployment to make the outbound-scope audit precise.

positives.title: Unconditional catastrophic-command floor with no override
positives.description: tools/approval.py enforces a hardline blocklist (filesystem-root wipe, home/system-dir recursive delete, mkfs, dd to raw device, fork bomb, kill -1, shutdown/reboot) that fires before any yolo/approvals-off/cron-approve setting and cannot be bypassed, matching the remit's Never-Allowed floor.

positives.title: Non-overridable provider-credential sandbox scrubbing
positives.description: tools/env_passthrough.py refuses to register Hermes-managed provider credentials as passthrough even when a skill or config requests it, preserving the execute_code/terminal sandbox's credential-scrubbing guarantee (fixes GHSA-rhgp-j443-p4rf).

positives.title: Fail-closed SSRF egress protection
positives.description: tools/url_safety.py resolves hostnames and blocks private/link-local/CGNAT targets and always-blocks cloud-metadata endpoints (including IPv4-mapped IPv6), failing closed on DNS or parse errors.

positives.title: Exact-pinned dependencies with OSV malware pre-check
positives.description: pyproject.toml pins every direct dependency to an exact version with CVE annotations, and tools/osv_check.py queries OSV for malware advisories before launching an MCP server via npx/uvx.

positives.title: Atomic 0600 credential files
positives.description: hermes_cli/auth.py creates credential and OAuth-token files atomically via os.open(O_EXCL) at mode 0600 with a 0700 parent, closing the TOCTOU window that a post-write chmod would leave open.

positives.title: Pairing-based gateway authorization (fail-closed to unknown users)
positives.description: The messaging gateway issues rate-limited, hashed one-time pairing codes to unknown users instead of serving them, with unauthorized-DM behavior defaulting to pair rather than open serving.

positives.title: Memory writes and loads scanned for injection/exfil
positives.description: tools/memory_tool.py runs the shared threat-pattern library over memory content on write (strict scope, blocking) and again when loading entries into the system prompt (blocked entries replaced with a placeholder), reducing the writable-memory persistence surface.

rows.content_type: free-form text, INFO+, redacted, gateway.* loggers only

raise_posture.weighted_rationale: Partial overall, but the label understates a posture that is Established across five of six categories and dragged down only by an intentionally broad domain. Zero Trust, Supply Chain, Red Team, Balance, and Monitor all rest on operative, layered controls — an unconditional command floor, fail-closed SSRF, exact dependency pins with OSV screening, a real adversarial test suite, injection scanning on ingress, and durable redacted logs — while Limit Your Domain is inherently weak for an agent designed to be omni-capable. The material gaps are concentrated in the approval layer's behavior outside recognized interactive/gateway contexts, not in missing controls; no unmitigated critical chain was found.

categories.name: Limit Your Domain
categories.rationale: The agent is deliberately general-purpose (terminal, code exec, browser, ~20 messaging platforms), so domain limiting reduces to operator-gated per-platform tool selection, swimlane definitions, and enforced non-goals (multi-tenant refusal, no unauthenticated serving) rather than a narrow scope; real structure exists but breadth is intentional.

categories.name: Balance Your Knowledge Base
categories.rationale: External content (web, messages, MCP responses, files, memory) is scanned by a shared injection/exfil/C2 pattern library with invisible-unicode detection — blocking on memory and skill writes, warning on tool results — and MCP tool descriptions are scanned for poisoning; the documented gap is that tool-result content still reaches context on a warn-only basis.

categories.name: Implement Zero Trust
categories.rationale: Layered and operative — an unconditional hardline floor, a sudo-stdin guard, a normalized 47-pattern dangerous-command detector with per-session approval, fail-closed SSRF, and non-overridable sandbox credential scrubbing — but the terminal/execute_code approval gate auto-approves in unrecognized non-interactive contexts (PRAX-2026-07-27-001) and its screening is pattern-based (PRAX-2026-07-27-002).

categories.name: Manage Your Supply Chain
categories.rationale: Direct dependencies are exact-pinned to ==X.Y.Z with CVE annotations in pyproject.toml, MCP extension packages get an OSV malware (MAL-*) pre-check before npx/uvx launch, and skills carry provenance plus an AST audit; no full ML-BOM and runtime lazy-install by PyPI name are the residual gaps.

categories.name: Build an AI Red Team
categories.rationale: A ~1300-file test suite includes a dedicated adversarial cluster (hardline blocklist, SSRF, prompt-injection, reply-to injection, fail-closed matrix approval, cron injection, security advisories) whose cases trace to named advisories (e.g. GHSA-rhgp-j443-p4rf) and issue-driven fixes, evidencing testing that changed the design rather than testing theater.

categories.name: Monitor Continuously
categories.rationale: Durable rotating logs (agent.log, errors.log, gateway.log) with a redacting formatter and usage/insights capture give operator-inspectable records, but the main logs are free-form text rather than a structured schema (PRAX-2026-07-27-005) and the tool-loop hard-stop is off by default, limiting automated detection.
